title: bundle install policy
description:
The rules a machine installs and updates bundles by (`bundle install`, `bundle update`, `bundle installed`).

Two files are read, and both apply: the machine's (/etc/bundle/policy.json, /Library/Application Support/bundle/policy.json on macOS, %ProgramData%\bundle\policy.json on Windows; BUNDLE_SYSTEM_POLICY overrides) and the user's (~/.config/bundle/policy.json, ~/Library/Application Support/bundle/policy.json on macOS, %APPDATA%\bundle\policy.json on Windows; BUNDLE_POLICY overrides).

When something new is installed, everything that vouches for it is gathered — its signature, and every attestation of its hash — and then:
• it is REFUSED if a requirement here (or a command-line flag) is not met, or an attester under `block` has marked it bad;
• it PROCEEDS if any of the evidence comes from someone accepted for this install before, someone under `trust`, or a certificate anchored in the trust store;
• otherwise the person installing is ASKED.

Requirements from every file and every `apps` section apply together (for a plugin, its `scopes` section instead of `apps`); trust adds up. Unknown settings are an error, so a typo cannot quietly loosen anything. `bundle policy` shows what is in force; `bundle policy check <file>` checks a file.

$schema.description: This schema, so an editor can help. `bundle policy init` writes it; nothing else reads it.

discovery.description: The backlink index asked who has attested a file — its `blue.microcosm.links.getBacklinks` endpoint — or false not to ask. The index only says whom to ask: every attestation it names is fetched from the attester's own PDS and verified. The user's setting wins over the machine's, except that a machine which turns discovery off keeps it off.

maxAge.description: How long a cached attestation proof counts after it was last confirmed — and so how long a withdrawn attestation can still be honoured by a machine that has not refreshed. Where both files set one, the shorter wins.

apps.description: Rules for one installed name — the name on your PATH, e.g. "pnpm" — on top of the global ones. They add requirements and trust; they cannot remove what the global rules require.

scopes.description: Rules for the plugins installed for one app (`bundle install --for <scope>`), by the app's package name — e.g. "bled" or "@acme/editor". They apply to those plugins on top of the global rules when they are installed, and on top of what the runtime carries over when an app that verifies its plugins loads them. They never apply to the app itself, and the app's `apps` section never applies to its plugins: the two have different authors.

rules.description: Rules for one installed name, or for the plugins of one app.

require.description: What must hold. An archive that does not meet a requirement is refused, never offered — so these are for decisions that should not be left to a prompt. Nothing an archive was installed with is a requirement by itself: a publisher who moves to another signer produces a question unless something here says otherwise.

signature.description: The archive must carry a signature that verifies — sigstore, from an issuer `issuers` accepts, or a certificate chain. Attestations alone are not enough.

sameIssuer.description: An update must be signed through the same OIDC issuer as the version it replaces — a release signed by GitHub Actions cannot be replaced by one signed by somebody's Google account. Applies once an install has a sigstore signature; says nothing about the first install.

attesters.description: Attesters that must have vouched for the archive (with a good verdict), as `did` or `kind@did` — the kind, when given, must match what they attested. Handles are not accepted here, because they can change hands; `bundle verify --attester <handle>` shows the DID.

quorum.description: How many of `attesters` must have vouched. Default: all of them. At most the number of attesters.

issuers.description: The only OIDC issuers whose sigstore signatures count at all; a signature through any other issuer is shown but cannot be accepted. Where several files or sections give a list, a signature must be in every one.

trust.description: Who is accepted without asking: evidence from these lets an install or update proceed. A bad verdict from anyone trusted here stops that and asks instead.

signers.description: Sigstore signers, matched exactly — identity and issuer both, never as a pattern.

identity.description: The signing identity (the certificate's subject alternative name): a workflow ref for CI, an email address for a person.

issuer.description: The OIDC issuer that vouched for the identity.

attesters.description: Attesters whose good verdict is accepted, as `did` or `kind@did` — with a kind, only attestations of that kind.

certificates.description: Certificate-chain roots, by SHA-256 fingerprint, for archives signed against a certificate authority of your own rather than sigstore.

block.description: DIDs whose bad verdict refuses an archive outright — at install and update, and at mount time through the cache (BUNDLE_BLOCK). A scanning service you rely on belongs here. A bad verdict from anyone not listed is a warning, since anyone can publish one.

ignore.description: DIDs whose attestations, good or bad, are not shown or counted.

did.description: A did:plc or a hostname did:web.

attester.description: An attester: a DID, optionally preceded by the kind of attestation required of it (`audited@did:web:audit.example.com`).

duration.description: A duration: `90s`, `30m`, `12h`, `7d`, or a bare number of seconds.
